Oct 21, 2026 3 min read

by

- Rafał Gancarz

#### Follow us on

The IT industry is changing before our very eyes. With AI entering the software architecture and development landscape, whether we like it or not, we are set to be taken on a roller coaster, the likes of which we haven’t seen since the advent of microservices and cloud-native computing. If the last decade was spent mostly on mastering and optimizing the cloud and micro- or nano-scale service-oriented architecture, the next decade will likely be spent figuring out how to master AI for building a new generation of IT systems.

These new systems will harness the power of AI in ways that, even today, are perhaps not fully comprehensible, as this space is moving forward at a neck-breaking pace, and last year’s best practice is this year’s antipattern. This rapid pace of innovation comes with many challenges, but can also be exciting for those willing to join the ride.

In this series, we try to establish agentic AI architecture as a new type of software architecture that will likely dominate the industry for years to come. The articles, written by industry experts, cover various elements and aspects of agentic AI architecture. We aim to present the latest trends and developments shaping the new type of architecture as it enters the mainstream.

While it’s impossible to characterize the new type of software architecture fully at this point, we hope this series offers useful insights into how the agentic AI space will shape the future of the IT industry in the coming years. Agentic AI Architecture is still in its infancy, but we hope to track how it evolves and matures and cover all key milestones and breakthroughs in the future.

# AI Changes the Data Interface, Not the Query Engine

Oct 22, 2026 16 min read

by

- Peihao Yuan

reviewed by

- Arthur Casals

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

### Key Takeaways

- An AI agent that reads Parquet still depends on an execution engine; AI changes the analytical interface and interpretation layer, not the need for precise computation.

- Separate deterministic computation from probabilistic reasoning. Engines should filter, aggregate, and join, while agents should interpret evidence and communicate conclusions.

- An embedded engine such as DuckDB can be sufficient when the data volume is moderate, the primary consumer is the agent workflow, and writes are controlled.

- A managed lakehouse becomes valuable when data has multiple independent consumers, must join with large shared datasets, requires concurrent writes, or needs organization-wide governance.

- Production-grade agent analytics should retain the source data, configuration, derived facts, and model outputs so that every report can be validated and replayed.

AI agents can now generate analytical code, read files from object storage, and turn operational data into structured reports. Does that make data lakes, lakehouses, and SQL engines obsolete? We encountered this question while automating the analysis of a large disaster-recovery exercise. Our first working design stored thirty-second service metrics as Parquet in S3-compatible object storage, used DuckDB for deterministic aggregation, and asked an AI agent to classify failover outcomes and explain the evidence. The prototype worked without a shared lakehouse, but not because the query engine disappeared. Instead, the engine became an embedded component inside the agent workflow. This article explains the architecture, introduces a practical separation between deterministic computation and probabilistic reasoning, and presents four signals for deciding when an embedded engine is sufficient and when a managed lakehouse is justified.

## The Question That Appeared After the Prototype Worked

The question did not come from a whiteboard exercise. It appeared after a real workflow successfully produced its first report. We were analyzing a disaster-recovery (DR) islanding exercise. During the exercise, one region was intentionally isolated, and traffic was expected to fail over to surviving regions. For every service, we needed to answer three questions:

- Did the surviving region absorb the traffic that left the isolated region?

- After absorbing the traffic, did the service remain available?

- Did latency remain within an acceptable range, or did the additional load create sustained degradation?

We exported service metrics at thirty-second resolution, wrote them as Parquet files to S3-compatible object storage, and let an AI agent generate a structured analysis report. Once the workflow ran end to end, an attractive idea emerged:

> If the agent can read files from object storage and produce the answer, why do we need tables, a catalog, a lakehouse, or SQL at all?

The question sounds reasonable because the user-facing experience has changed. Instead of opening a dashboard or writing a query, an engineer asks the agent to analyze the exercise. The agent identifies the relevant data, generates DuckDB SQL or Python as needed, executes the analysis through deterministic tools, and explains what happened. For example, to verify whether traffic shifted from Region A to Region B during failover, the agent may generate a read-only DuckDB query over a predefined set of tables and time ranges. Before execution, the query is validated against an allowlist of accessible datasets and operations, then executed in a sandboxed analysis runtime. The runtime returns structured query results, which deterministic application code normalizes into a fact packet containing fields such as traffic volume by region, timestamps, and percentage changes. A simplified implementation looks like this query:

generated_sql = """ SELECT region, SUM(request_count) AS requests FROM traffic_metrics WHERE ts BETWEEN :start_time AND :end_time GROUP BY region """ validate_sql( generated_sql, allowed_tables={"traffic_metrics"}, allowed_operations={"SELECT"}, ) rows = sandbox.execute( generated_sql, params={ "start_time": exercise_start, "end_time": exercise_end, }, ) fact_packet = { "metric": "request_count", "window": [exercise_start, exercise_end], "by_region": { row["region"]: row["requests"] for row in rows }, }

In this simplified example, the agent generates only the analytical query. A deterministic validation layer rejects access to non-allowlisted tables or non-read-only operations before execution. The query then runs in a sandboxed runtime and the returned rows are converted by application code into a structured fact packet. The model receives this packet (for example, request counts for Regions A and B) rather than inventing or directly estimating those values.

## Why DR Analysis Is More Than Scanning Metrics

The difficult part of DR analysis is not retrieving a time series. It is deciding what the time series means. Suppose Region A is isolated and Region B remains active. A healthy failover should produce a recognizable sequence:

- QPS decreases in Region A.

- QPS increases in Region B by a corresponding amount.

- The success rate in Region B remains above the service objective.

- Tail latency may rise briefly, but it should not remain elevated.

Each statement requires context. A QPS increase is not automatically a successful failover. It may be too small to account for the traffic lost in the isolated region. A lower success rate is not automatically a DR failure if the metric includes expected business rejections. A latency spike at the cutover boundary may be harmless if the system quickly returns to a steady state. We therefore used two baselines and a steady-state window:

- Historical baseline. the same time window on the previous day, which captures normal time-of-day behavior.

- Immediate baseline, the hour before the exercise, which captures the most recent service state.

- Steady-state window, a post-cutover interval that excludes the short transition period and focuses on sustained behavior.

The analysis collected four core signal families:

- qps

- err_qps

- success_rate

- latency_pNN, including tail latency such as p99

For each service, deterministic code calculated facts such as traffic absorption ratio, SLO violations, latency change, and the duration of sustained degradation. The agent then interpreted those facts in the context of the service, the exercise configuration, and the available evidence. This distinction is fundamental. The hard part is often the judgment, but the judgment is only trustworthy when the facts underneath it are deterministic.

## Architecture: Object Storage, an Embedded Engine, and an Agent

The workflow used three logical layers: data preparation, deterministic computation, and agent-driven interpretation, with reproducibility treated as a cross-cutting requirement. The data-preparation layer used reusable DuckDB build logic, which was generated once and then reused, to transform raw metrics into self-describing assets in object storage. For each analysis request, the agent selected the relevant inputs, generated constrained SQL or Python, and orchestrated deterministic execution in DuckDB/Python. The resulting structured fact packets were then interpreted by the agent to produce the final report. Throughout the workflow, the input data, configuration, reusable build logic, deterministic facts, and agent execution metadata were retained so that the analysis could later be reconstructed, replayed, and evaluated.

Figure 1. The AI agent initiates and orchestrates the analysis, deterministic tools compute the facts, and the agent interprets the resulting fact packet. Source: Authors’ own illustration, created with assistance from ChatGPT.

### Storage and Self-Description

The physical data lived in S3-compatible object storage. Each exercise had a self-describing directory:

s3://<bucket>/<root-prefix>/ index.json <exercise-id>/ manifest.json exercise_config.json metrics-*.parquet service_dimension.parquet

The files served different purposes:

- index.json listed available exercises.

- manifest.json recorded the schema, row counts, file sizes, and checksums.

- exercise_config.json captured time windows, regions, thresholds, and exercise identity.

- metrics-*.parquet contained the thirty-second metric facts.

- service_dimension.parquet contained service metadata such as ownership and service tier.

The manifest was important because a folder of files is not yet a trustworthy data asset. Consumers need to know what is present, which schema was used, whether the write completed, and whether the files can be validated later.

## Deterministic Processing with DuckDB

DuckDB was used on both sides of the storage boundary. During ingestion, it read the raw metric records, sorted them, wrote compressed Parquet files, and generated validation statistics for the manifest. During analysis, it read the Parquet files directly, filtered the relevant windows, joined service metadata, and computed the fact packet used by the agent. This architecture benefited from several properties of DuckDB:

- It runs in-process, so it can travel with the agent workflow instead of requiring a separate database service.

- It reads Parquet directly and can push filters and column selection into Parquet scans.

- It provides SQL semantics for aggregation and joins.

- It can spill larger operations to local storage instead of requiring the entire working set to remain in memory.

The point was not that DuckDB is universally better than Spark , Trino , or a managed lakehouse. The point was that the workload did not yet need a shared distributed engine.

### Probabilistic Interpretation with the AI Agent

The agent did not receive hundreds of thousands of raw metric rows and attempted to count errors or average latency itself. Instead, it received a compact, deterministic evidence packet for each service. A simplified packet looked like this example:

{ "service_id": "service-a", "exercise_window": "post-cutover-steady-state", "expected_failover_qps": 1200, "observed_qps_increase": 910, "traffic_absorption_ratio": 0.758, "success_rate_baseline": 0.9992, "success_rate_during_exercise": 0.9941, "service_slo": 0.9990, "p99_latency_baseline_ms": 84, "p99_latency_during_exercise_ms": 191, "sustained_degradation_minutes": 18, "data_quality_flags": [] }

The agent used the packet to classify the outcome, explain the supporting evidence, and propose the next investigation step. A corresponding output might be:

{ "classification": "partial_failover", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [ "The surviving region absorbed approximately 76% of the expected traffic.", "Availability remained below the service SLO during the steady-state window.", "The p99 latency increase was sustained for 18 minutes." ], "recommended_action": "Review routing capacity and downstream dependency limits." }

The exact numbers came from the engine. The model's responsibility was to determine how those numbers should be interpreted and communicated.

A simple threshold-based rule was not always sufficient. For example, a service might temporarily exceed its p99 latency threshold immediately after cutover while traffic had already shifted correctly and availability remained within the service objective. A rule that treated any threshold violation as a failure would classify the service as degraded. The agent could instead compare the transition window with the steady-state window, recognize that latency returned to baseline within a few minutes, and classify the event as a successful failover with transient degradation rather than a sustained DR failure.

# From Microservices to Agents: The Next Evolution of Distributed Systems

Oct 19, 2026 12 min read

by

- Mallika Rao

reviewed by

- Rafał Gancarz

#### Follow us on

### Key Takeaways

- Agentic AI systems shift distributed systems design from orchestrating services to orchestrating decisions made at runtime.

- Unlike microservices, agentic systems introduce non-deterministic execution paths driven by context, reasoning, and tool selection.

- Decision quality becomes a first-class reliability concern alongside latency, availability, and throughput.

- Production failure modes often manifest as silent degradation in reasoning quality rather than explicit system errors.

- Effective agentic architectures require bounded autonomy, evaluation loops, and hybrid deterministic fallback systems.

## Distributed Systems Are Entering a New Phase

Over the past decade, microservices have reshaped how large-scale software systems are designed and operated. They enabled teams to decompose monoliths into independently deployable services, scale ownership boundaries, and evolve systems incrementally. For many organizations, microservices became the dominant model for building distributed systems at scale.

At their core, microservices solved a fundamental problem: how to decompose functionality across services and teams in a way that supports independent evolution while maintaining system reliability. They introduced explicit service boundaries, well-defined APIs, and predictable execution flows.

#### Related Sponsors

A new architectural shift is now emerging, driven by advances in large language models (LLMs) and reasoning systems. Rather than focusing on decomposing functionality, this new paradigm focuses on decomposing decisions. Systems are beginning to move from static orchestration models toward adaptive, runtime decision-making systems. This is the foundation of what is increasingly referred to as agentic AI.

Agentic systems differ from traditional services in a fundamental way. Instead of executing predefined logic, they dynamically determine which actions to take, which tools to use, and how to sequence multi-step reasoning processes. Execution is no longer fully specified at design time; it emerges at runtime based on context, goals, and intermediate outcomes.

This shift introduces new capabilities. Systems can become more adaptive, more context-aware, and better able to handle ambiguous or evolving inputs. At the same time, it introduces new forms of complexity that are not well addressed by traditional distributed systems thinking.

The goal of this article is to explore this transition in depth: how agentic AI architectures differ from microservices, what architectural patterns are emerging, what failure modes we are beginning to observe in production systems, and how observability and reliability practices must evolve. The discussion is grounded in experience operating large-scale distributed systems in domains such as search, recommendation, and serving infrastructure.

## Microservices Solved Service Decomposition — Agents Solve Decision Decomposition

Figure 1: Execution Model: Microservices vs Agentic Systems (Source: created by the author with OpenAI ChatGPT)

[Click here to expand image above to full-size ]

Microservices architecture introduced a clear model for structuring distributed systems. Instead of a single monolithic application, systems were decomposed into services aligned with business capabilities. Each service owned a bounded context — a clearly defined domain of responsibility and data ownership — communicated via APIs, and could evolve independently.

This decomposition enabled faster deployment cycles, clearer ownership boundaries, and improved scaling characteristics. However, despite their flexibility, microservices still rely on deterministic execution. The control flow of a request is explicitly defined through service-to-service interactions.

In a typical microservices-based system, a request follows a well-understood path: it enters a service, is processed, calls downstream services in a defined sequence, and returns a response. Even in highly complex systems, the execution path is known in advance and encoded in the system's logic.

Agentic AI systems introduce a different model of execution. Instead of defining the full sequence of operations upfront, systems determine execution paths dynamically. Decisions about which tools to invoke, which data sources to query, and which strategies to apply are made at runtime.

This represents a shift from service decomposition to decision decomposition. Rather than distributing functionality across services, systems distribute reasoning across components that participate in a dynamic decision loop.

In practice, this means that execution is no longer a fixed pipeline but an adaptive process. A system may choose different candidate sources depending on context, dynamically adjust ranking strategies, or re-evaluate outputs based on intermediate results. The structure of execution becomes contingent on both input and evolving system state.

This change has profound implications for how we reason about distributed systems. It introduces flexibility but also reduces predictability. It replaces static workflows with dynamic reasoning paths, which are inherently more difficult to trace and debug.

## What Makes Agentic Systems Fundamentally Different

Figure 2: Agentic System Architecture (Source: created by the author with OpenAI ChatGPT)

Agentic systems differ from traditional distributed systems in three key dimensions: control flow, state management, and failure semantics.

Control flow is no longer fixed. In microservices architectures, execution paths are designed and encoded ahead of time. In agentic AI systems, execution paths are determined at runtime based on context and intermediate reasoning. This introduces flexibility but also variability in system behavior, since different requests may trigger entirely different execution paths depending on user intent, retrieved information, or prior decisions made during execution.

The state also becomes more fluid and less strictly defined. Traditional systems rely on explicit state transitions and well-defined persistence models. Agentic systems, by contrast, often operate over an evolving execution context that is continuously updated as reasoning progresses. This context may include conversation history, intermediate plans, retrieved documents, ranking signals, tool outputs, or prior evaluation results.

Managing this evolving context becomes a core systems concern. Context often must propagate across multiple agents, tools, and services while remaining sufficiently consistent to support coherent downstream reasoning. In practice, many systems introduce shared context stores, execution-scoped memory, or structured reasoning artifacts to avoid context fragmentation and contradictory decisions across execution steps. As execution chains become longer, context management begins to resemble distributed state coordination problems seen in earlier generations of distributed systems.

Failure semantics also change. In traditional systems, failures are typically binary: a request succeeds or fails, a service responds or times out. In agentic systems, failures often manifest as degraded decision quality. The system may continue to operate but produce suboptimal outcomes due to incorrect reasoning, poor tool selection, stale context, or incomplete interpretation of intermediate results.

These differences fundamentally change how distributed systems behave in production environments. They also require new architectural patterns to manage complexity, reliably propagate context, and maintain predictable system behavior at scale.

## Architectural Patterns in Agentic AI Systems

As agentic systems begin to appear in production environments, several architectural patterns are emerging. These patterns are not formal standards but rather recurring structures that help manage complexity and control variability in decision-making systems.

One common pattern is the separation of planning and execution responsibilities. In this model, a planning component is responsible for interpreting intent and determining a high-level strategy, while execution components perform deterministic operations such as data retrieval, transformation, or ranking. This separation allows systems to isolate non-deterministic reasoning from deterministic execution, improving reliability and traceability.

A second pattern involves the specialization of agents. Instead of relying on a single general-purpose agent, systems are increasingly composed of multiple specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct capability such as retrieval, ranking, evaluation, or orchestration. These agents collaborate to produce final outcomes.

This structure resembles service decomposition in microservices architectures, but applied to decision-making rather than data processing logic. While specialization improves reasoning quality and modularity, it also introduces coordination overhead and increases system complexity. Latency becomes more variable, and failure modes can propagate across agent interactions.

A third pattern is the integration of evaluation directly into execution loops. Instead of treating evaluation as an offline process, systems increasingly evaluate outputs during runtime. Based on evaluation results, systems may dynamically refine, retry, or adjust strategies.

This introduces feedback loops into execution, enabling more adaptive behavior. However, it also requires careful control to avoid excessive retries or runaway execution cycles. Constraints such as latency budgets, iteration limits, and confidence thresholds become essential for maintaining system stability.

A further emerging pattern is the introduction of tool abstraction layers. As agents interact with a growing number of services and APIs, teams are creating standardized interfaces for tool use. These abstraction layers decouple agent reasoning from underlying service implementations and provide a consistent mechanism for capability discovery and invocation.

Over time, this abstraction layer begins to resemble a platform for capabilities rather than a collection of individual services. It becomes a critical enabler for scaling agentic systems across teams and domains. Across these patterns, a consistent theme emerges: complexity is shifting from service orchestration to decision orchestration. Systems are no longer primarily concerned with how services interact, but with how decisions are made, evaluated, and adapted over time.

## Failure Modes in Agentic Distributed Systems

Figure 3: Silent Failure Modes in Agentic Systems (Source: created by the author with OpenAI ChatGPT)

Agentic systems introduce new failure modes that differ significantly from those observed in traditional distributed architectures. While microservices typically fail due to latency, availability issues, or data inconsistencies, agentic systems often fail due to degraded decision quality.

One important failure mode is cascading decision degradation. In traditional pipelines, failures propagate through explicit dependencies. For example, if a system selects suboptimal candidate sources early in execution, subsequent ranking and evaluation steps operate over reduced-quality inputs, amplifying the initial error.

# From Reusable to Regeneratable: Rethinking the Shared UI Component Library

Oct 02, 2026 15 min read

by

- Daniel Curtis

reviewed by

- Daniel Bryant

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

### Key Takeaways

- Regeneration has changed the economics of reuse. A model pointed at a solid design system can produce most standard UI on demand, so paying to keep a canonical component package alive is much harder to justify than it once was.

- Keep the design system, tokens, guidelines, and tests central. They are what actually buy you consistency.

- Regenerated code must be verified before you trust it; visual-regression, accessibility, and token-conformance tests do that job.

- Left to their defaults, models converge on a bland average, which is exactly why an opinionated design system becomes a differentiator.

- Accessibility, genuinely hard widgets, and cross-team functional consistency are still good reasons to keep some curated, shared code.

For most of the last decade, one piece of advice went almost unquestioned inside any growing engineering organization and that was to build a company-wide component library. If you put your buttons, modals, data grids, and form controls into one versioned package, then every team inherits consistency, accessibility, and speed. It felt built into our DNA; reusability is good for consistency and speed. This idea is worth revisiting in 2026. The advice was good previously, but the conditions that made one shared library the obvious call have since changed. When a coding agent can produce a styled, more-or-less accessible component in little time, keeping one canonical library for a whole company buys less than it once did. For many organizations, the shared library is now needed less. What is worth centralizing is the design system, the tokens, the guidelines, and the tests, but not the shipped component code.

This centralization is something with which we have hands-on experience at Griffiths Waite. We have spent most of the last decade building shared UI’s in React, maintaining component libraries and design systems across large enterprise clients. We have seen the benefits libraries can bring, and now we are starting to rethink what the future of component libraries and design systems look like.

## What the Library Was Really For

A shared library always bundled four separate promises into one artifact:

- Reuse, so nobody builds a date picker for the fifth time.

- Consistency, so one team's button, table, or form control behaves like the next team's, which is very important for consistent experiences.

- Encoded expertise, so accessibility, keyboard handling, the unique cases specific to an organization, and the awkward edge cases are solved once, by people who care.

- A single source of truth, so a brand change lands everywhere from one place.

Out of the four, only two actually need shipped code. Consistency and source-of-truth belong with a design system and its design tokens , the shared color, type, and spacing values a component merely references. Reuse and encoded expertise are what justified the package itself, which are exactly the parts AI can now help with.

## Maintenance Is the Real Bill

The initial build of a library was always time consuming, whether it was built during a Sprint Zero or as a dedicated project, but the expensive part of a shared library is never the first release. It is the decade afterwards. Once consumers start using it you have a bunch of applications you are now supporting and needing careful considerations when making changes.

In a piece on abstraction ownership at daisyUI, they outline:

> Every line of code you own, is a line you have to maintain, test, fix, and update.

This assertion is why in any abstraction, following guidelines like Avoid Hasty Abstractions (AHA) can be beneficial, because abstracted code needs to be maintained and often the cost of maintenance is not worth the abstraction. Choosing what to abstract is becoming even more important when writing or rewriting code is easier and cheaper than it ever has been.

A heavily upvoted Hacker News thread , which looks into how you can roll out an internal UI component library, received a comment from someone who suggested avoiding component libraries; his company was on its second attempt to roll one out:

> Internal UI component libraries are expensive to produce and maintain – they're much more complex than your average CRUD app and require skilled, disciplined people to actually pull off, as you have to think years into the future and have as little staff rotation as possible.

When adoption spreads from one product team into others, ownership becomes tricky, maintainers are pulled into other delivery work, priorities clash between consumers, and teams building against it produce every multiple variants of a component when they need only two or three. You end up having to run the library as a fully fledged project with backlogs, alignment sessions, and planning, all of which is overhead, the tax you keep paying for years after the first release.

We have experienced this problem first-hand at Griffiths Waite running shared libraries across large, multi-team environments. Once a library is adopted widely, dependency management becomes a balancing act, keeping multiple versions of components aligned so the single source of truth doesn't quietly fragment as teams drift onto different versions. Upgrade rollouts are difficult when shared components wrap specific third-party libraries. Bumping or swapping out those dependencies is difficult to untangle. Every consumer has to be migrated in step rather than at its own pace. Even a well-intentioned change can ripple into every consuming app, so versioning and communication end up mattering as much as the code, and a component tends to accumulate more variants than any single consumer needs. The entire shared library only stays healthy with clear, sustained ownership, which is exactly the attention that slips when maintainers are pulled onto other delivery work.

This sustained ownership doesn’t make shared libraries worthless. A company-wide library is a product with a roadmap, support load, deprecation policy, and a team. Starve that team and within a couple of release cycles every downstream project is patching around a library nobody owns.

## Regeneration Became Cheaper Than Reuse

Reuse won for many years and the reason is clear. Rebuilding was slow and error-prone, so writing one good implementation and spreading the cost across every consumer was obviously the smart move. Generative AI changes this set of problems. When the implementation cost is less, the focus can shift higher to the areas that drive the need for centralized design systems in the first place.

Marco Kotrotsos, in an essay he titled The Death of the Component Library , describes how Tailwind's own paid-component business was undercut by its own ubiquity: Because Tailwind is so heavily represented in training data, "when developers need a Tailwind component, they don't visit the documentation. They prompt. The AI generates the code directly". The standardization a library sells turned out to be the very thing that made the library redundant as a way to ship code.

Denis Uraev frames this change as a move from reusable to regeneratable code . Keep the specification, regenerate the implementation when you need it, and lean on tests that let agents "verify correctness independently". A 2026 technical report on component-based development for AI coding makes the same case from the research side, describing tooling that helps agents "inspect, modify, test, debug, and regenerate code fragments".

If a team can quickly generate the components it needs from a shared design system and a well-defined prompt, a central package it has to version, publish, and upgrade is worth far less. Consistency still holds, because the design system now carries it.

## Centralize the Rules, Generate the Parts

To be clear, this approach asks for more discipline, not less. It just moves that discipline from the code to the rules. The center of gravity moves from a shared code artifact to a shared set of constraints, which are still artifacts.

Start with the design system and its tokens as the single source of truth. Teams already treat tokens this way, running one definition through tooling like Style Dictionary to produce CSS, iOS, and Android values. Tokens are cheap to keep alive and they are exactly the kind of structured input a model handles well.

Then move on to machine-readable guidelines. Design-system teams are already feeding models persistent rules (e.g., token usage and accessibility requirements) kept in a versioned directory beside the code, then running audit prompts to catch hardcoded values and contrast failures. These guidelines form the new component library, so instead of code, you receive the core instructions.

Engineering principles, the sort captured in plain language to provide opinionated defaults with conscious deviation, keeping one definition and zero drift across generated and hand-written code, and treating accessibility as non-negotiable , are exactly the persistent constraints a model needs before it writes anything. Griffiths Waite has a good example of this approach, a principle library covering a wide range of engineering rules that manage component simplicity, developer experience, and accessibility. It is the first thing we would now point a coding agent at. Kept as a searchable, discipline-organized library rather than tribal knowledge, these libraries become reusable input for every regeneration.

The combination of design system, tokens, component instructions, and engineering principles are the specification with which an agent generates components. Each project generates what it needs against those rules, tuned to its own framework version, while skipping the components it will never use instead of dragging around an entire library.

With regeneration from designs, we are already relying on this approach in our projects at Griffiths Waite; we use the Figma MCP server and have found it remarkably accurate at generating UI directly from Figma designs. We combine this use with the skills we created and added to our projects to encode our engineering best practices and keep the generated code aligned to our standards rather than whatever a model would produce by default.

The final step is verification. How can you trust the generated code? Visual-regression tools including Chromatic, Percy, and Playwright diff a component against an approved baseline and catch the wrong shade of blue or the four-pixel padding drift that unit tests miss. The Playwright CLI can work for this problem. It is possible for the agent to compare the build against a Figma design via the MCP server and perform screenshot comparison testing between the two to ensure they align. The same tool can assert that regenerated markup still matches the required accessibility structure , while computed-style checks can confirm color, spacing, and type resolve to tokens.

## Change Control Moves Up the Stack

If the rules are now the product, the question is how you version them. With a shared library, change control lived in the shipped code. A release is published with a new version, consumers bump a dependency and migrate, with semantic versioning (SemVer) signaling how much would break. With regeneration, the shipped code is disposable, so versioning moves up to the artifacts from which every regeneration reads.

The engineering skills, the crosscutting principles to include accessibility, component simplicity, and developer experience, can be versioned on their own cadence separately to the component library. These skills should sit across all of the codebases and be managed independently.

# Composable Commerce: Inside Shipt’s Kit Platform

Oct 14, 2026 16 min read

by

- Khurshid Hameed

reviewed by

- Rafał Gancarz

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

### Key Takeaways

- A commerce platform tends to age better when it is built from a small number of first-class entities that reference each other rather than duplicate data between them. The pull to introduce a new entity for every new use case is constant, and it usually signals that the existing model needs to flex rather than grow.

- When a feature has to satisfy several independent constraints at once — which locations can serve a customer, which offerings are enabled where, which categories carry extra eligibility rules — treating the problem as an intersection of independently-evaluated sets scales better than threading conditional logic through a single workflow.

- Grouping related items under a shared identity, with its own completeness guarantees, keeps a bundled offering from silently degrading into something that no longer matches what was promised to the customer.

- Regulated or constrained product categories are easier to support safely when their constraints are modeled as a distinct type carrying its own rules, rather than as flags scattered through a shared code path. New categories then become additive, rather than compounding the complexity of existing ones.

- When a fully safe editing workflow is not realistic within a launch deadline, a layered set of lighter-weight guards can capture most of the risk reduction at a fraction of the engineering cost — often enough of a trade-off to ship safely under real time pressure.

## The launch

Kits at Shipt are built for moments — a game day, a holiday dinner, a hosting weekend. The window between a merchandiser deciding to launch a themed bundle and a customer needing it can be days, not weeks. Every architectural decision described below is downstream of that constraint.

In June 2026, Shipt launched Shipt Kits, a one-click cart-building feature designed to help customers plan their hosting events. Timed around a global soccer event, the company’s national brand campaign introduced Shipt Kits through a celebrity partnership, highlighting summer use cases such as watch parties, backyard hosting, and cookouts. Customers landing on a "Match of the Week" kit could add a full evening’s worth of groceries — sides, drinks, snacks, dessert — to their cart in one click. Each item was store-aware: the kit you saw at your store reflected what was actually on shelves near you, not a generic catalog.

The campaign was covered in Progressive Grocer, Supermarket News, ¡HOLA!, and Better Homes and Gardens. From the outside, it looked like a polished new feature.

From the inside, the team had three weeks to build it. The API was done in ten days. The remaining eleven went to the admin experience, the customer surfaces, and the operational hardening that turns a working prototype into something a merchandising team can use without supervision.

This is an architecture tour of what was built in those three weeks: how the platform replaced a multi-day clerical workflow with a single admin UI, how it was modeled as three first-class entities that compose well, how the catalog was made store-aware end-to-end, and how it was made safe to edit live without a full draft-publish lifecycle.

Figure 1. Platform architecture overview (Image source: created by author)

The Kit API sits between the merchandiser-facing admin UI and the entity layer, with store-aware resolution and kit-type compliance rules determining what a customer ultimately sees, and edit-safety guards protecting in-flight changes.

## Before Kits: a manual assembly workflow

Before Kits, building a themed shopping experience at Shipt looked like this. A merchandiser who wanted to assemble, say, a Tailgate Bundle would:

- Query the data warehouse for products that fit the theme.

- Pick the relevant UPCs by hand from the query results.

- Translate each UPC to the retailer-specific product ID — different IDs for the same physical product at Target, Meijer, Publix, and so on.

- Build a category containing those retailer-specific IDs.

- Build a product list from that category.

- Plug the product list into wherever the bundle needs to show up.

After all that work, the bundle still wasn’t guaranteed to display correctly at every store. The workflow was pegged on product ID, not on per-store inventory, so a kit that looked complete in the admin tool could be missing half its items at the customer’s actual store. The merchandiser had no way to know in advance.

Figure 2. The pre-Kits workflow: six manual steps and no per-store guarantee (Image source: created by author)

For a one-off promotion that lived for a week, this was tolerable. For a national campaign that needed dozens of fresh kits launching on cadence — across multiple retailers, multiple regions, multiple weeks — it was impossible. When the campaign got the green light with a fixed launch date, the team had three weeks to build a system where merchandisers could describe a bundle once and have the platform handle the per-store, per-retailer materialization.

## Three first-class entities: items, shopping lists, kits

The first architectural decision was the most important: model the platform as three composable entities, not one monolithic "kit" type.

The approach draws on the design vocabulary of Domain-Driven Design (DDD). Items , shopping lists , and kits form the ubiquitous language shared across code, admin UI, and merchandiser conversations, and each is modeled as an aggregate that owns its own invariants. Kits act as aggregate roots for editorial and structural metadata; items live in their own bounded context and are shared by reference rather than duplicated inside every kit that uses them. Naming these boundaries early kept downstream feature work — new kit types, ad monetization, per-store resolution — additive rather than disruptive.

Items are the atomic catalog units — generic, typed, and tagged. An item knows what kind of thing it is (a product, an ingredient, a non-product element of an editorial bundle) and carries arbitrary metadata in a JSON tag bag. Items are not retailer-specific; the resolution to a particular store’s product ID happens at view time, not at modeling time.

Shopping lists are curated sequences of items. A shopping list can be merchandiser-curated and attached to a kit (the "here’s what to grab for your party" list inside a Game Day Bundle) or customer-built (a personal grocery list that the customer maintains across sessions). The same shopping-list abstraction supports both, which means the platform maintains one mental model and one set of APIs rather than two parallel ones.

Kits are the composable bundles — the things customers see, click, and add to cart. A kit carries editorial metadata (title, description, hero image, theme), structural metadata (slot layout, type, anchor items), and references to items and optionally to shopping lists.

Figure 3. Items as a single source of truth, referenced by both shopping lists and kits (Image source: created by author)

The platform’s most consequential property is that items are shared by reference across shopping lists and kits. The same Heinz ketchup item powers the Tailgate Bundle, the Backyard BBQ Bundle, the Family Picnic Bundle, the customer’s personal grocery list, and twenty other surfaces. Updating the item’s metadata propagates everywhere it’s used. Adding a new retailer mapping for that item lights it up across every kit and list that references it, automatically.

An item, roughly, looks like this:

{ "id": "itm_01H2N7X...", "item_type": "product", "canonical_name": "Heinz Tomato Ketchup, 20 oz", "tags": { "category": "condiments", "dietary": ["vegetarian", "gluten-free"], "seasonal": ["summer", "grilling"], "brand_id": "brand_heinz" } }

The tags field is intentionally a schemaless JSON bag — new dimensions (dietary, seasonal, promotional, anything a merchandiser or downstream service wants to filter on) can be added without a migration. Retailer-specific product IDs deliberately don’t live on the item; they’re resolved at view time, per store, which is the subject of the next section.

The migration that unified items into this single source of truth — kit products and shopping-list items both pointing at the same item rows — was mechanically boring but paid off immediately. Maintenance dropped. New kit types became inexpensive to introduce because a new type just needed to know which items it references, not how to manage its own private item table.

## Anchor items and kit identity

A kit is more than a bag of items. Some items are essential to the kit’s identity. A summer grilling kit without meat is not a summer grilling kit. A pasta-night kit without pasta is not a pasta-night kit. An alcohol kit without alcohol is, legally and conceptually, something else.

The team modeled this with the concept of anchor items . An anchor item is one whose absence — at a specific store, on a specific day — disqualifies the entire kit from being shown at that store. The merchandiser marks anchor items during kit creation. The resolution layer checks anchor availability before deciding whether to surface the kit.

Anchor items also drive a per-kit minimum product threshold. A kit can declare that it needs at least, say, eight non-anchor items available at the customer’s store to be worth showing, in addition to all anchor items being present. The thresholds and anchors compose: a kit is shown only if (a) every anchor item resolves at the store and (b) the total available item count clears the threshold. As a result, the platform never shows customers a half-empty kit. The kit either makes sense at this store today, or it doesn’t appear in the customer’s catalog at all. For a curated, editorial product, this is the contract the team wants.

## Resolving a kit per store, per customer

Figure 4. The customer’s effective retailer set is the intersection of three independently configured layers (Image source: created by author)

Behind every customer view of a kit is a small set-theoretic computation that decides which retailers’ inventories to query. A customer at a given zip code may be served by a set of grocery retailers—the customer’s local Hy-Vee, Target, Meijer, and Giant Eagle. Each kit has its own allow-list of retailers it’s enabled for. Some kits—alcohol kits, most notably— also have additional eligibility constraints that depend on store-level licensing.

The resolution is the intersection of all three:

effective_retailers = customer_zip_retailers ∩ kit_allowed_retailers ∩ kit_eligibility(store)

For an alcohol kit, the eligibility check filters to stores with active alcohol licenses in the customer’s jurisdiction. For a kit with no special eligibility, the third set is unconstrained. For a general national-campaign kit, the allow-list covers Shipt’s operational areas. Each layer is independently configurable; the intersection is computed very efficiently at request time.

Once the effective retailer set is known, the platform fans out concurrent searches against each retailer’s catalog, collects the results, and assembles the customer-facing kit. Items are scored against the retailer’s actual inventory, anchor items are checked, the minimum threshold is verified, and the kit is either rendered or quietly dropped from the customer’s view.

The fan-out matters operationally. A customer at a metro zip might be eligible for four retailers; the kit needs to materialize quickly enough to feel instantaneous. Sequential per-retailer queries would have been too slow at the latency budgets the team was targeting. Concurrent fan-out, with per-retailer timeouts and graceful degradation, keeps the customer-perceived latency flat regardless of how many retailers the customer is eligi

# Agents Refactor 300K Lines in Three Weeks, and Practitioners Ask What it Proves

Sep 30, 2026 4 min read

by

- Steef-Jan Wiggers

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

CodeScene has published a case study in which coding agents refactored a 300,000-line C codebase over three weeks, at a token cost of roughly $4,000. The work produced 2,903 commits across 726 files, modified 252,055 lines, and moved the codebase from a Code Health score of 5.6 to 10.0. The codebase is Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike, taken from an open-source decompilation.

Adam Tornhill, CodeScene's founder and the author of Your Code as a Crime Scene, wrote that this was the first time he had seen what he called superhuman AI performance at scale, after three decades working on large systems.

Two mechanisms carried the work. The first was a quality signal: the CodeHealth MCP Server , which gave agents a deterministic score to optimize and to judge whether a transformation had helped. The second was correctness: a replay-trace harness that compared the rollback state hash frame by frame, so behavior could be checked after every change.

The more novel result is what the agents built along the way. Rather than applying a fixed catalogue, they accumulated a refactoring playbook, ending with 22 recipes and 82 supporting notes. Familiar transformations appear, including Extract Function and Guard Clauses, but so do recipes specific to this codebase. Shared Index Range captures repeated loops differing only in start and end ranges. Action Parameter handles duplicated control structures differing mainly in which function they invoke. Uniform Step Table converts heterogeneous calls into table-driven dispatch. Failed attempts were recorded too, including transformations that made Code Health worse.

Model choice mattered. The team settled on Claude Opus for the bulk of the work, reporting that Claude Code with Opus was significantly better than Codex with Sol at capturing and documenting the emerging patterns. Files often plateaued when smaller models ran the task, appearing to reach a local optimum they could not move past.

Non-merge commits per day by model across the three-week project (Source: CodeScene )

Reaction from practitioners on LinkedIn has been sharply divided, and the split runs along what the result proves rather than whether it happened.

Paolo Perrone put the case for taking it seriously:

> most refactor claims i've read rest on a green test suite, which only tells you the tests survived. replaying traces against a fighting game sets a much higher bar.

Mats Iremark, CTO at Omda Response, reported doing something comparable, writing that the CodeScene MCP combined with current agents is almost like cheating.

The skeptics concentrated on scope. Konrad Otrębski, a tech lead and consultant, asked whether the work was merged, whether it arrived as one enormous merge or many, and whether this was an experiment on open-source code rather than production code earning money. Daniel Webb, CTO at NeoSee and one of the two engineers who did the work, replied that it was merged to main on a fork, through 54 pull requests.

Otrębski's follow-up set a higher bar:

> I think the real true test of AI capability here would be to offer this courtesy of refactoring to some famous open source project, say Grafana. The definition of done is ofc merging it to master.

Tracy Bannon, a software architect and researcher, objected to the framing rather than the method, noting that describing the outcome as perfect is pretty bold.

Denis Baltor questioned the discovered recipes themselves, arguing that DRY concerns duplication of knowledge and intent rather than identical lines of code, and that recipes defined by loops differing only in ranges, or control structures differing only in the function invoked, may be collapsing the two.

Asko Nõmm raised the methodological question. Since Claude Code and Codex are tuned to their own models, he argued it is unclear how much of the result measures the model and how much measures the harness, and that cost would vary the same way. He added that architecture remains unmeasured, so code can look healthy while fundamental problems surface later.

Several unanswered questions came from the authors themselves. Marc Bouvier asked whether non-functional behavior had improved, given that framerate, memory use and input latency matter in a game; Webb said a performance specialist was being brought in. Asked whether the harness caught subtle frame timing regressions, he said there might be no definitive answer, because it ran as a pre-commit hook and some failures were fixed without being observed. On diff sizes, he was equally direct: if you are not familiar with the code and no longer review every line, how big can a diff be? He made no assertion, only questions.

If these reactions are representative, the disagreement is not about the numbers, but about the conditions that produced them. The replay-trace harness worked because a decompiled game offers deterministic frame-by-frame replay. Most legacy systems have no equivalent oracle, which is the same reason refactoring them is risky in the first place. Tornhill writes that automated tests and equivalence checks are absolutely essential safeguards, which places the burden on exactly the thing unhealthy codebases tend to lack.

The team's own selection process illustrates it. Webb said they considered a Gov.UK marine licensing codebase he had worked on, but it was too healthy to be useful for the research that follows, and chose the game partly because they play it and are therefore its users.

That research is the next step. The uplift produced two functionally equivalent versions of the same system, one at Code Health 5.6 and one at 10.0, for a study with Lund University in which students will implement features in both using frontier models and compare cost and quality.

Two headline figures belong to that future work rather than this case study. CodeScene projects a roughly 70% reduction in AI-induced defects and roughly 45% less token waste from the uplift, both extrapolated from its earlier research rather than measured here. The $4,000 and the three weeks were measured.

Recently launched, Amazon CloudWatch Omni is an AI-first observability platform designed to monitor, evaluate, and troubleshoot applications and autonomous AI agents in a unified environment.

For traditional applications, metrics such as latency, errors, CPU and availability are often sufficient to identify operational problems, says AWS senior specialist solutions architect Daniel Abib. For AI agents, an execution can succeed technically while still producing the wrong result , using the wrong tool, retrieving poor information, or taking an unnecessarily expensive path:

> Agent behavior is non-deterministic: a prompt change can degrade response quality even when standard metrics show no errors. Teams spend hours manually reviewing logs across multiple systems, unable to pinpoint what changed or why.

To address this challenge, Omni captures end-to-end traces, evaluates correctness, coherence, retrieval, and tool selection, and lets you compare prompts, build test datasets from production traffic, run experiments, and detect regressions.

It supports several agent frameworks, including LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI SDK, Strands, and Vercel AI SDK. It also uses open standards such as OpenInference and AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) and integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. For evaluations, CloudWatch Omni also supports third-party evaluators such as Braintrust, DeepEval, and Ragas.

Amazon CloudWatch Omni provide unified observability , bringing traditional microservices, cloud infrastructure, and generative AI/agentic workloads under the same umbrella for a unified view. It offers native OpenTelemetry support, allowing existing telemetry to feed into Omni without complex reconfigurations, as well as dual workspaces, which provide a standalone web experience for operators via single sign-on (SSO) outside the traditional AWS Management Console, alongside a free, local, developer-friendly IDE extension supporting both VS Code and Kiro.

CloudWatch Omni also support AI-powered investigations, allowing users to query logs, metrics, and traces using natural language to identify topology issues and pinpoint root causes.

AWS vice president Chet Kapoor summarizes the new tool on LinkedIn saying that it "helps you catch issues proactively, trace them to their root cause, and identify improvements across your agents, applications and infrastructure in one place". Former AWS principal security consultant Jorg Huser, similarly notes that "A unified view that explains why an agent acted the way it did is the only way to keep confidence intact at scale".

As a final note, Deutsche Bank lead devops engineer Florin Lungu emphasizes that CloudWatch Omni "supports open standards and built-in evaluators for quality assurance".

While CloudWatch Omni may be the natural fit for applications running on AWS, several other observability tools and platforms combine tracing, evaluation, prompt experimentation, and datasets, with a focus on agentic applications. Akka used 65 open source projects to test a spec driven workflow for AI assisted software porting, measuring specification structure, context, model and effort selection, automated validation, token consumption, and runtime performance. The initial tranche took 99.3 hours and consumed 9.41 billion tokens, with Akka reporting a lines of code or performance improvement in 57 of the 65 ports.

The experiment used two tranches. Akka analyzed all 65 projects, generating specifications and implementing up to 10% of each project's surface area, then selected 10 for complete implementation based on system characteristics and measurable results. The delivery harness cycled through discovery, specification, porting, benchmarking, and improvement. Discovery analyzed code, models, schemas, and runtime behavior, while Claude with Akka Specify handled implementation, testing, and review. A common benchmark runner compared tests, code size, and latency.

Akka delivery harness workflow(Source: Akka Blog Post )

Akka found that structured specifications with claims, evidence, and typed behavior improved first-pass implementations, while gaps in context files remained around cross-component decisions. Follow-up areas include interface enumeration, test ingestion, provenance tracking, differential testing, and adversarial testing. GitHub Spec Kit similarly structures coding agent workflows around specification, planning, tasks, implementation, and convergence. In Akka's experiment, Sonnet averaged 61 minutes per port versus 120 minutes for Opus, while Opus used about 40% fewer tokens. Higher effort settings increased consumption without consistently improving efficiency.

The finding prompted discussion among engineers following the research. Aaditya, commenting on Tyler Jewell's CEO of Akka LinkedIn post , wrote

> Smaller model's behavior matched modernization work he had observed, where the small model follows the spec while a larger model may improvise.

Aaditya also questioned

> Whether reductions in lines of code resulted primarily from dead code removal or from differences in the target language.

Rick Bryce , Head of Marketing at Avahi, raised a related point in the same discussion and suggested that constraints could influence the result. The comments add questions around whether model capability, specification constraints, or both account for differences in porting efficiency.

> Cheaper model giving the tighter port is the finding worth chasing

Akka model and effort efficiency chart (Source: Akka Blog Post )

Validation used the original unit and integration tests alongside auditors checking serialization, security, error handling, PII, idempotency, and architectural boundaries. Akka added guardrails as failures exposed new issues, while reporting that additional exit conditions increased porting costs. Performance varied by project: applications, frameworks, and libraries generally improved, while infrastructure and tooling showed median degradation. Google has released Android Bench 2.0 , a major update to its benchmark framework for evaluating AI models and agents on Android development tasks. The update introduces long-horizon tasks (LHTs), agent-based evaluation, and continuous scoring to better assess performance on complex, multi-step development tasks.

Launched a few months ago , Android Bench evaluates AI models against a set of common development tasks and incorporates Android best practices in areas such as permissions, navigation, and connectivity. With the latest release, Google has expanded the benchmark to cover a broader range of development tasks.

> Today we're releasing the first set of long-horizon tasks (LHT), which are tasks of great complexity that take an engineer multiple days or even a week to complete. We are also introducing agentic evaluation, starting with agents from corresponding model providers.

While the original version focused on incremental changes to existing repositories, Android Bench 2.0 introduces long-horizon tasks (LHTs) that Google describes as work an engineer might take "multiple days or even a week to complete". These tasks include upgrading dependencies, adding new features, building apps from scratch, or converting a cross-platform app to Android.

One major change in version 2.0 is the shift from binary pass/fail evaluation to a more nuanced scoring system. Previously, a complex task could be marked as failed because of a single failing edge-case assertion, even if the agent had successfully met dozens of other requirements.

> We calculate this completion rate through a combination of factors like functionality, visual fidelity, and avoiding regressions. We also apply objective scoring penalties for deviations from evaluation instructions or structural constraints.

Android Bench 2.0 results also help identify which tasks are more likely to succeed with AI assistance. For example, Google reports that "AI does a better job at writing new code rather than refactoring existing code", which may reflect that refactoring and migrations require an understanding of the codebase's architectural complexity.

Similarly, AI performs well on several "well-established, deterministic transformations", even in larger codebases. Examples include converting Java to Kotlin, swapping Retrofit for Ktor, or introducing a ViewModel layer.

In contrast, models still struggle in many cases, including tasks requiring runtime validation (like missing dependency injection graphs), breaking framework changes, or knowledge gaps with unreleased libraries. In particular, the best-in-class model achieves only an 80% completion rate in porting a cross-platform app to Android, which remains overall an "open challenge".

The updated Android Bench 2.0 dashboard includes recent models, such as Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, OpenAI GPT-6, Anthropic Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8 Max. At the time of the article, Claude Opus 5.5 was at the top of the leaderboard with a 32% LHT pass rate, followed by GPT -6 Astra at 28%.

# Google Antigravity SDK Adds Local Model Support for Greater Token Efficiency and Code Privacy

- Reading list

Google has introduced support for local models in the Antigravity SDK , enabling developers to build and execute agentic workflows directly on their own machines, while retaining the flexibility to mix in cloud-based models for higher-level tasks. This approach gives developers greater control over data privacy, inference costs, network dependencies, and computational workload distribution.

One of the most compelling capabilities of the Antigravity SDK is hybrid agent orchestration, which adapts Google's proposed Architect-Builder pattern to a mixed cloud-local compute environment.

According to the Architect-Builder pattern, one primary, high-context AI agent, the architect , holds the macro-level system view, including dependencies, architectural guardrails, and detailed specifications or implementation plans. Once the architect has defined a plan, several parallel, multiple specialized AI agents, the builders , work independently in isolated environments to execute discrete, narrow tasks mapped out by the specification.

Google says that the Antigravity SDK enables the architect to operate in the cloud, devising a strategy and breaking the task into smaller units using filenames and task descriptions, without requiring access to the source code itself. The builders, instead, run locally and perform tasks such as reproducing security vulnerabilities, proposing code fixes, reviewing candidate patches, and running regression tests. Additional specialized local agents can validate proposed changes against the provided test suites, keeping the code-intensive stages of the workflow on-device.

In a demonstration involving the auditing and patching of three vulnerable Python modules, Google reports that only 95 out of approximately 3400 tokens were used on the cloud for planning, while the remaining 97.2% were spent locally. Google also states that no source code was uploaded to the cloud.

The initial implementation focuses on running Gemma 4 26B A4B through Google's LiteRT technology. However, developers are not limited to LiteRT exclusively, as the Antigravity SDK also supports OpenAI-compatible local inference servers through LocalOpenAIAgentConfig , including Ollama, LM Studio, and vLLM.

Commenting on the announcement, Reddit user ambassadortim highlighted that "companies can have more control over their AI model and when to change or at least have more control over that". In a separate discussion, FollowingTop3534 questioned whether the cloud-token share metrics tells the whole story :

> I'd benchmark patch acceptance, wall time, and energy alongside the cloud-token share. '97.2% of tokens ran locally' is interesting, but it doesn't tell you whether the run was faster or cheaper on your hardware, and the recommended 24GB+ VRAM or unified memory is a real gate.

As a final note from the community, user Latter_Crazy expressed enthusiasm comments on the new capabilities:

> it can do things I could not do before with the cloud rules. Cost, speed, quality are all going up and this is just the start. Highly recommend looking into this.

The Antigravity SDK should not be confused with the Antigravity IDE , which is an IDE powered by the Antigravity SDK. They share the same underlying agent infrastructure, but serve different purposes, with the SDK letting you build your own AI agents programmatically rather than simply using them for coding tasks.

# Microsoft Commits Maia to Multi-Gigawatt Inference, and its Efficiency Metric Draws Questions

Oct 16, 2026 4 min read

by

- Steef-Jan Wiggers

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Microsoft will scale its Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia "the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services." The architecture behind that commitment is unusually specific about data movement. The efficiency claim leading the announcement is not, and practitioners have said so.

Maia 200 is already in production , serving Microsoft Copilot and the MAI team, with GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry to follow by the end of the year. It is deployed across the United States, Europe, and Australia, and Microsoft says it delivers up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt for built-in AI in Teams and Copilot than leading GPU infrastructure. Maia 300 begins production deployments in 2027.

Maia 300 is inference-first, aimed at long-context, memory-intensive, and decode-heavy work rather than training, which neither announcement mentions. Each accelerator carries eight HBM4 stacks, providing 288 GB and 18 TB/s within a 950-watt TDP. A rack holds 96 accelerators in 167 kW across 24 four-accelerator trays, reaching 27.6 TB of HBM and 1.7 PB/s aggregate. Compute chiplets are built on TSMC N2P, with memory-controller and I/O functions on separate dies, which Microsoft says raises compute FLOPs by 36% and contributes to 2.5 times the memory bandwidth and roughly twice the HBM bandwidth per watt of Maia 200. Memory organization moves from uniform access to a NUMA layout across chiplets so software can place data near the compute using it.

The networking is where the design is most opinionated. Maia’s AI network controller implements a custom AI transport built on Ethernet, and Microsoft describes the result as "one fabric rather than separate scale-up and scale-out domains." Accelerators initiate communication to any peer in a superpod "without involving the host or a discrete scale-out NIC." Two accelerators are directly linked within a tray, a switched fabric joins all 96 in a rack, and optical second-tier switches connect up to 128 racks into a superpod of 12,288 accelerators. The post names three latency domains: a direct pair, one hop within the pod, and three hops across pods, and expects software to keep tensor-parallel traffic in the lowest. The split between in-rack and cross-rack bandwidth is "not fixed at the system design time" but set by job packing, which is how an accelerator can drive up to 750 GB/s to any peer when only a subset cross racks.

That fabric carries a specific inference pattern. Prefill and decode workers are sized and placed independently, and after prefill completes, KV state "moves directly to the selected decode workers over the same scale-up fabric rather than leaving the domain through a separate host-mediated scale-out path." The same fabric lets a spare tray in one rack offset a failed tray in another, transparently to software kernels.

Microsoft’s headline figure is that it expects Maia 300 "to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems," alongside up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput and more than 2.5 times the performance per watt of Maia 200.

That figure is what drew reaction, and the objection was to the unit rather than the number. Rick Bullotta wrote the most-engaged comment on Satya Nadella’s announcement post :

> "Tokens per watt";. What an absurd metric. As if there’s a uniform, consistent definition of a token or a generic correlation to compute. Not. And such a metric would inherently reward verbosity.

Commenter Michel Floyd put the dimensional version in one line: "Shouldn’t it either be tokens per second per watt or tokens per KWh?" Vinay Bansal, founder of UBIQS and building a competing inference accelerator, questioned the workload the figure was measured on:

> 40% more tokens per watt, but at what context length? The workloads you named, sustained multi-step agents, carry long contexts, and every agent’s working memory grows with each step. At that point the binding constraint is memory, not compute, and the specs that lead this launch are memory specs.

If these reactions are representative, the architecture will be easier to assess than the claim. Microsoft never names the GPU systems it compares against, and its own framing is that Maia 300 maximizes "useful tokens per watt and useful tokens per dollar," without defining what makes a token useful. The announcements also differ in confidence: Scott Guthrie and the engineering post say Microsoft expects the 40% improvement, while Nadella’s post states that it delivers it.

A second question concerns who gets access. Every workload named across both posts is Microsoft’s own, including Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Foundry, the MAI team, and Dragon Copilot, and neither post says customers can provision Maia capacity directly. Phillip Pham, chief executive of Pexon Consulting, asked, in German, whether the gains translate into cheaper provisioned throughput reservations or whether the hardware stays reserved for Microsoft’s own services, since with committed capacity it is the price per guaranteed token that decides the benefit in production.

Microsoft has not published a technical paper beyond the engineering blog post by Rani Borkar and Saurabh Dighe, which the announcement links to. Microsoft says it will share more at Microsoft Ignite 2026 in San Francisco next month.

# Cloudflare Uses an AI Harness to Probe and Harden its WAF

Oct 07, 2026 2 min read

by

- Matt Foster

#### Follow us on

- Reading list

Cloudflare placed frontier AI models inside a controlled testing harness to probe its Web Application Firewall (WAF), using blocked attacks as starting points for models to generate and refine new variations.

Across 45 scenarios, the system generated 1,107 attempts and left 49 findings after human triage. The exercise ultimately contributed to three changes in Cloudflare’s Managed Ruleset.

The experiment began with attack payloads that the WAF had already blocked. Rather than repeatedly replaying fixed test cases, model calls proposed changes to their encoding, placement, or delivery based on responses from earlier attempts. The models had no access to Cloudflare’s WAF rules, source code, or internal security signals, making the test effectively black-box from their perspective.

A Python harness handled the parts Cloudflare did not want to delegate to the models. It constructed and replayed HTTP requests, maintained scenario state, enforced limits, and collected responses. One model call proposed the next mutation while another reviewed the resulting response, allowing subsequent attempts to adapt without giving the models direct control over request execution.

One SSRF test illustrates how that feedback loop worked. The tester repeatedly changed the representation and placement of a cloud metadata address, trying decimal, octal, and other forms. Eventually, a request using a decimal representation was blocked. On the next attempt, the model retained the same request shape but switched to a trailing-dot representation of the address; this time the client encountered a redirect rather than a WAF block. Cloudflare preserved the result for investigation rather than treating it as evidence that the attack had succeeded.

Source: Cloudflare

That distinction proved important at scale. Of the 1,107 recorded mutation attempts, 607 produced the post-triage result set: 558 requests blocked by the WAF and 49 findings considered relevant for further remediation work. Forty-eight of the 49 findings involved command injection or server-side request forgery (SSRF).

Human review remained the final validation step. Reviewers checked whether requests had actually reached the target, remained malicious, were clearly unblocked, fell within the WAF’s responsibility, and could be safely reproduced. Surviving cases were then replayed and evaluated as candidates for changes to rules, normalization, or other mitigations.

The work contributed to three changes in Cloudflare’s Managed Ruleset: two new detections, SSRF - Obfuscated Host and SSRF - Restricted Protocol, alongside an improvement to the existing SSRF - Cloud rule.

The same harness pattern appears elsewhere in security engineering. While Cloudflare’s Vulnerability Discovery Harness separates vulnerability discovery from independent validation, Google Mandiant’s Agentic Vulnerability Discovery Harness chains specialised agents through source-code analysis, hypothesis generation, and verification before findings reach human reviewers.

"Agentic Vulnerability Discovery Harness Chain" - Source Google

Other systems use different terminology but follow a similar discovery-and-validation pattern. OpenAI’s Codex Security builds a threat model for a repository, searches for vulnerabilities, and attempts to reproduce candidates in an isolated environment before proposing fixes for human review. Google’s PageBreak similarly focuses on validating whether AI-generated vulnerability hypotheses are actually exploitable, partly to prevent security teams being overwhelmed by plausible but unverified findings.

Across these systems, the common thread is the harness around the model: constraining execution, preserving state, validating findings, and turning probabilistic exploration into evidence that existing security workflows can use.
